title: Libro de los juegos de ajedrez, dados y tablas
shelf_note: A photograph of an illuminated 13th-century Castilian manuscript of Alfonso X's book of games: a chess problem with a miniature. That matches the title, author, date and language. No tradition or collection is given to test it against.
structure_note: The structure count of pages_translated (0) disagrees with the book field (189). Only 34 of 219 pages carry a printed number. The leaf numbers are small hand-written folio numerals in the top corner, so the 4 backsteps and 2 repeats are more likely misread numerals than a splice. This leaf shows folio '8' at page record 26, which fits a book with front matter or unfoliated leaves.

pages.layout: large miniature across the top (four players around a chessboard), two text columns below, red rubric, a decorated blue-and-red initial L, running head in red and blue capitals, and a strip of the facing leaf's text at the left edge

items.quote: A rectangular miniature painting framed in grey, set agains
a 'divided game,' a set chess problem
the counselor, precursor of the modern queen
the 'elephant,' precursor of the modern bishop

missing.english: that is in the third square of the white alfferza
missing.why: medieval descriptive notation: squares are named by the file of a piece's starting square, counted from that side's back rank. Without a note a reader cannot place any move.
this contradicts the mate in four that follows. A reader needs to know what the number counts, or that the numeral is uncertain.

missing.english: the white king must take it by force with his alffil
missing.why: 'the white king' here means the white side, not the king piece. Read literally, the sentence makes no sense.

book_verdict: This is the right leaf, a real 13th-century manuscript, on the right shelf. The translation is faithful and recovers the sense where the OCR misreads 'prieto' as 'puesto' throughout. One embarrassment is visible on sight: the miniature's description is shown as an editorial <note>.
